name: Mississippi

code.name: Mississippi Code of 1972 Annotated, Title 23, Chapter 15 (the Mississippi Election Code), and sections 140 to 143 of the Mississippi Constitution of 1890
code.edition: not read as a Code: the Code's own publisher (LexisNexis, linked from the Legislature's home page) was not requested. Each section is read, where possible, in the text of the Act of the Legislature that last printed it, on the Legislature's bill-status host: HB 467 of 2017 (the Election Code revision, in force 1 July 2017), SB 2144 of 2024, HB 293 and HB 291 of 2025; the Constitution only as the Legislature's proposal HC 47 of 2020. Sections for which no printing act was found are read in the Secretary of State's PDF of Chapter 15 printed with the 2017 session laws, a lower grade. Acts of 2018 to 2026 were looked through for later changes (see notes).
code.site: https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/ (bill and resolution texts of the Mississippi Legislature); https://www.legislature.ms.gov/

ms-sos-code.citation: Miss. Code Ann. Title 23, ch. 15, as the Secretary of State publishes it (PDF, the 2017 printing), read for the sections that no act of the Legislature read here prints: 23-15-781, 23-15-783, 23-15-921, 23-15-923, 23-15-927, 23-15-955
ms-sos-code.note: A PDF of the whole Election Code on the Secretary of State's own site; the statute's own words in the 2017 printing (every page footer reads '2017 By the State of Mississippi and Matthew Bender & Company'), but not a page of the Legislature's, so graded as an agency publication. Amendments made after July 1, 2017 are not in it. Kept as the source only where no act of the Legislature printing the section was found (see the other sections and the notes).

ms-county-handbook.citation: Mississippi Secretary of State, 2026 County Elections Handbook (the page footers read 'Rev. 12/24/2025'; the file name says 'revised 12-26-2025'), part on general and special elections
ms-county-handbook.note: An agency handbook, not the statute. Used here only for what it says of mistakes in a canvass (a commission cannot reopen its certification; a court corrects it). Its statement of the county tie rule is the pre-2025 rule (23-15-601 before House Bill 291 of 2025) and is no longer used.

ms-hc47-2020.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2020 Regular Session, House Concurrent Resolution 47, as adopted by the House and Senate (proposes to amend section 140 of the Mississippi Constitution of 1890 and to repeal sections 141, 142 and 143; to go to the voters on 3 November 2020)
ms-hc47-2020.note: The HTML rendition of the resolution on the Legislature's bill-status host (documents/2020/pdf/HC/HC0047SG.pdf is the same document; I read both). In the HTML the words that the resolution strikes out stay in the text beside the new words, so quotations are taken only from sentences that the resolution adds or from its title and resolving clauses. It is the proposal, not the voters' result (see unread). The Legislature's history page for HC 47 (https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/2020/pdf/history/HC/HC0047.xml, read 2026-11-07T08:13Z) shows the resolution adopted by both houses on conference report (28 and 29 June 2020) and the enrolled resolution signed on 1 July 2020; it shows nothing of the vote of the electors.

ms-hb291-2025.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2025 Regular Session, House Bill 291 as sent to the Governor (approved 24 March 2025; in force 1 July 2025): Miss. Code 23-15-193 and 23-15-601 as amended, 23-15-603 and 23-15-605 brought forward, 23-15-951 as amended
ms-hb291-2025.note: The HTML rendition on the Legislature's bill-status host. It prints the words the act strikes out beside the words it adds (the PDF, ms-hb291-2025-pdf, shows a '* * *' where words are struck and leaves them out). So every quotation here is either of a passage the act leaves untouched or is cut with [...] at the place where words were struck, and the struck words in 23-15-601 are shown in ms-hb291-2025-pdf. The act prints 23-15-193 twice: as it reads 'Through December 31, 2024' and as it reads 'From and after January 1, 2025'; only the second is quoted for the present rule.

ms-hb291-2025-pdf.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2025 Regular Session, House Bill 291 as sent to the Governor, the PDF of the same act
ms-hb291-2025-pdf.note: Used only to show which words the act strikes: the PDF prints '* * *' where words are struck and omits them. Its text carries the bill's line numbers, so quotations from it are short and cut at line ends.

ms-sb2144-2024.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2024 Regular Session, Senate Bill 2144 as sent to the Governor (approved 13 May 2024; runoff and second-primary timing in force 1 January 2025): Miss. Code 23-15-191, 23-15-193, 23-15-833 and 23-15-981 as amended
ms-sb2144-2024.note: The HTML rendition on the Legislature's bill-status host; the struck words ('three (3)') stay in the text beside the new ones ('four (4)'), so the quotations are cut with [...] at the place of the change.

ms-hb293-2025.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2025 Regular Session, House Bill 293 as sent to the Governor (approved 17 April 2025; in force 1 July 2025): Miss. Code 23-15-1031 (congressional primaries) as amended
ms-hb293-2025.note: The HTML rendition on the Legislature's bill-status host (struck words stay in the text beside the new words).

ms-hb467-2017.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2017 Regular Session, House Bill 467 'Election code; revise', as sent to the Governor (approved 18 April 2017; in force 1 July 2017 for the sections used here): Miss. Code 23-15-171, 23-15-607, 23-15-611, 23-15-857, 23-15-911, 23-15-1033 and 23-15-1041 as amended
ms-hb467-2017.note: The act that revised the Election Code in 2017. The HTML rendition prints struck words beside the new ones, so quotations are cut with [...] where the act strikes words. No later act amending these sections was found (see the notes for how I looked); where one is found it is a different section here (23-15-193, 23-15-601, 23-15-605, 23-15-833, 23-15-951).

ms-hb1310-2023.citation: Mississippi Legislature, 2023 Regular Session, House Bill 1310 as sent to the Governor (approved 19 April 2023): new Miss. Code 23-15-615 (audit of election procedures)
ms-hb1310-2023.note: The HTML rendition on the Legislature's bill-status host. Read for what the procedural audit is and when it comes: the Secretary of State audits election procedures in all 82 counties, in no more than 25 percent of the precincts or five precincts in each county, whichever is less, and not if the election is challenged under 23-15-927, 23-15-951 or 23-15-955.

ties.applies_to: U.S. Representative in the general election (a congressional district is made of two or more counties)
ties.steps: the Secretary of State sums the county returns; if candidates standing highest and not elected have an equal number of votes, each candidate draws one of two sealed containers from an opaque bag, under the direction of the Governor and the Secretary of State; the containers hold a straw of conspicuous length and a shorter straw, and the candidate drawing the longer straw is declared the winner
ties.who: the Governor and the Secretary of State

sources.quote: if it appears that two (2) or more candidates for any district office where the district is composed of two (2) or more counties, standing highest on the list, and not elected, have an equal number of votes, the election shall be decided between the candidates having an equal number of votes by each candidate individually drawing one (1) of the two (2) sealed containers from an opaque bag, under the direction of the Governor and Secretary of State.
The containers shall consist of a straw of conspicuous length, and the candidate drawing the container with the longer of the two (2) straws shall be declared the winner.
The laws regulating general elections shall [...] apply to and govern elections for representatives in Congress

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-605, as the Legislature's House Bill 291 (2025) brings it forward unchanged; the straw draw replaced a draw of lots in the 2017 revision (HB 467). 23-15-605 does not name Congress: it names 'any district office where the district is composed of two (2) or more counties', and 23-15-1033 (HB 467, 2017) sends congressional elections to 'the laws regulating general elections'. That a congressional district is such an office is my reading [inferred]. The majority-and-runoff rule of 23-15-193 does not reach this election: it is for the offices of the odd-year state general election.

ties.applies_to: U.S. Senator in the general election
ties.steps: no tie clause naming a U.S. Senator was found; the Code says a Senator is elected 'in the same manner' as Representatives

sources.quote: There shall be elected, by the qualified electors of Mississippi, [...] one (1) United States Senator at the same time and in the same manner that members of the lower house of Congress are elected

ties.note: Read: 23-15-1041 (quoted), 23-15-1033 (HB 467, 2017) and 23-15-605 (HB 291, 2025). The straw-draw clause of 23-15-605 names 'any district office where the district is composed of two (2) or more counties'; a Senate seat is statewide, so the clause does not name it. Whether 'in the same manner' carries the Representatives' straw draw to a Senate seat is not said [inferred; not decided here]. This is a search of those sections, not a finding that the law has no rule.

ties.applies_to: the offices elected at the state general election of 2023 and every fourth year after (23-15-193(1)): Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Auditor, State Treasurer, Attorney General, public service and transportation commissioners, Commissioner of Insurance, Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce, senators and members of the House of Representatives, district attorneys, circuit and chancery clerks, sheriffs, coroners, assessors, surveyors, members of the boards of supervisors, justice court judges and constables, and all other officers elected at the general state election (not municipal offices, judges of the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals, or special elections)
ties.steps: a candidate who receives a majority of the votes cast for the office at the general election is elected; if none does, the two candidates with the most votes go on the ballot for a runoff four weeks later (three weeks until 1 January 2025), and the candidate with a majority of the runoff votes is elected; if no one has a majority and two or more are tied for the next highest vote, all of those tied and the highest candidate go on the runoff ballot, and whoever receives the majority of the runoff votes is elected

sources.quote: TO REQUIRE ALL CANDIDATES RUNNING IN THE STATE GENERAL ELECTION TO SECURE THE MAJORITY VOTE TO BE ELECTED

there shall be elected a Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, Auditor of Public Accounts, State Treasurer, Attorney General, three (3) public service commissioners, three (3) Mississippi Transportation Commissioners, Commissioner of Insurance, Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce, Senators and members of the House of Representatives in the Legislature, district attorneys for the several districts, clerks of the circuit and chancery courts of the several counties, as well as sheriffs, coroners, assessors, surveyors and members of the boards of supervisors, justice court judges and constables, and all other officers to be elected by the people at the general state election.
candidate that receives a majority of votes cast for the office at the general election shall be elected.

If no candidate receives a majority number of votes cast at the election, then the two (2) candidates who receive the highest number of votes cast shall have their names placed on the ballot for the runoff election to be held four (4) weeks later.
The candidate who receives a majority of the votes cast in the runoff election shall be elected.

However, if no candidate receives a majority vote cast at the election, and there is a tie in the election of those receiving the next highest vote, then those candidates receiving the next highest vote and the candidate receiving the highest number of votes cast shall have their names placed on the ballot for the runoff election to be held [...] four (4) weeks later, and whoever receives the majority of votes cast in the runoff election shall be elected.
(2)   The * * * candidate that receives a majority of votes
If no person receives a majority of the votes, then a runoff election shall be held under procedures prescribed by the Legislature in general law.

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-193(2), as House Bill 291 (2025; in force 1 July 2025) prints it 'from and after January 1, 2025'. The act prints the older reading too ('Through December 31, 2024', with 'three (3) weeks'), whose first sentence of subsection (2) says 'The state officers that receive a majority'; HB 291 changed those words to 'The candidate that receives', and its long title describes the change as requiring 'all candidates running in the state general election' to secure the majority vote. The Legislature's list of measures of 2025 gives its short title as 'County and county district officers; require to have runoff election if no candidate receives majority after general election.' (https://billstatus.ls.state.ms.us/2025/pdf/all_measures/allmsrs.xml, read 2026-11-07T08:13Z). So a majority and a runoff now plainly apply to the Governor and the other statewide officers, to legislators and to county officers alike; that the second sentence ('If no candidate receives a majority') already reached further than the first before HB 291 is possible and is not settled by the text [inferred]. For the Governor and the statewide officers, section 140 of the Constitution as HC 47 (2020) proposed it leaves the runoff to 'procedures prescribed by the Legislature in general law' and abolishes the old election by the House of Representatives (section 141); whether the voters adopted HC 47 on 3 November 2020 was not read (see unread). The next state general election with these offices is 2027. Justice court judges' runoffs are under 23-15-981 (subsection (3), next rule but one).

ties.applies_to: the same offices (23-15-193(1)), when two or more candidates have an equal number of votes after the runoff
ties.steps: the interested candidates appear before the Chief Justice of the Mississippi Supreme Court within two days after the canvass, and the tie is determined by a toss of a coin or by lot fairly and publicly drawn; a certificate of election is then given
ties.who: the Chief Justice of the Mississippi Supreme Court

sources.quote: If it appears that two (2) or more candidates for [...] office have an equal number of votes after the runoff election, the interested candidates shall appear before the Chief Justice of the Mississippi Supreme Court within two (2) days after the canvass and the tie shall be determined by a toss of a coin or by lot fairly and publicly drawn, and a certificate of election shall be given accordingly.
or more candidates for * * * office have an equal number of votes

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-193(2), last sentence, as HB 291 (2025) prints it. Until HB 291 the clause read 'candidates for state office'; HB 291 struck the word 'state' (the PDF shows '* * *' in its place), so the clause now reads 'candidates for office' [measured from the PDF; the effect on legislators and county officers is inferred]. This is the Governor's tie rule: the runoff first, then the Chief Justice with a coin or a lot (a rule of the Code, not of the Constitution, which carries none). It overlaps with 23-15-601 and 23-15-605 for legislative seats (next two rules): the act changes both and does not say which controls after a runoff.

ties.applies_to: state Representative, and State Senator where the county is a senatorial district, for a district of one county or part of a county
ties.steps: the interested candidates appear before the county election commissioners within two days after the canvass, and the tie is determined by a toss of a coin or by lot fairly and publicly drawn; a certificate of election is then given

sources.quote: the interested candidates shall appear before the election commissioners within two (2) days after the canvass and the tie shall be determined by a toss of a coin or by lot fairly and publicly drawn, and a certificate of election shall be given accordingly.
The foregoing provisions shall apply to Senators, if the county be a senatorial district.
or more candidates for Representative of the county, or part [...] of the county * * * standing highest on the list, and not elected,

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-601(1), as HB 291 (2025) amends it. HB 291 struck from the clause the words 'or for any county office, board of supervisors, justice court judge or constable' (the HTML shows them struck; the PDF shows '* * *'), so the clause now names only Representatives of the county or part of it; county officers are left to the runoff and Chief Justice rule above. The subsection still says the certificate goes 'to the person having the greatest number of votes' for a one-county legislative seat, while 23-15-193(2) now asks a majority and a runoff of senators and members of the House; the act changes both and does not say which controls, in particular whether the commissioners' toss or the Chief Justice's decides a tie that remains after a runoff [inferred: both clauses stand; which governs is not stated]. Each house also judges the election of its own members (see the recount rules), so a seat can be taken up by the house after either.

ties.applies_to: state Representative or State Senator for a district made of two or more counties
ties.steps: the Secretary of State sums the county returns; candidates with an equal number of votes each draw one of two sealed containers from an opaque bag under the direction of the Governor and the Secretary of State; the longer straw wins
ties.who: the Governor and the Secretary of State

sources.quote: if it appears that two (2) or more candidates for any district office where the district is composed of two (2) or more counties, standing highest on the list, and not elected, have an equal number of votes, the election shall be decided between the candidates having an equal number of votes by each candidate individually drawing one (1) of the two (2) sealed containers from an opaque bag, under the direction of the Governor and Secretary of State.
The containers shall consist of a straw of conspicuous length, and the candidate drawing the container with the longer of the two (2) straws shall be declared the winner.

shall sum up the whole number of votes given for each candidate other than candidates for state offices, legislative offices composed of one (1) county or less, county offices and county district offices

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-605, brought forward unchanged by HB 291 (2025). 'Any district office' is read as including a legislative district [inferred]; the same section takes 'legislative offices composed of one (1) county or less' out of the Secretary of State's count, which implies that a legislative district of more than one county is in it. Like the previous rule, this overlaps with the runoff and Chief Justice clause of 23-15-193(2), which the same act changed and which names senators and members of the House; the act does not say which governs after a runoff.

ties.applies_to: judge of the Supreme Court or the Court of Appeals, in the general election (judicial elections are nonpartisan)
ties.steps: a candidate with a majority of the votes cast is elected; if none has one, the two with the most votes go on the ballot for a second election four weeks later (23-15-981); if candidates standing highest and not elected have an equal number of votes, the State Board of Election Commissioners, summing the county returns, decides between them by each drawing one of two sealed containers from an opaque bag under the direction of the Governor and the Secretary of State, the longer straw winning (23-15-607(1))
ties.who: the Governor and the Secretary of State

sources.quote: if it appears that two (2) or more candidates for judge of the Supreme Court or Court of Appeals standing highest on the list, and not elected, have an equal number of votes, the election shall be [...] decided between the candidates having an equal number of votes by [...] each candidate individually drawing one (1) of the two (2) sealed containers from an opaque bag, under the direction of the Governor and Secretary of State.
The containers shall consist of a straw of conspicuous length, and the candidate drawing the container with the longer of the two (2) straws shall be declared the winner.

If no candidate for such office receives a majority of the votes cast for such office in the general election, the names of the two (2) candidates receiving the highest number of votes for such office shall be placed on the ballot for a second election to be held [...] four (4) weeks later in accordance with appropriate procedures followed in other elections involving runoff candidates.

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-607(1) as the 2017 revision (HB 467, in force 1 July 2017) prints it, and 23-15-981 as SB 2144 (2024) amends it. No later act amending 23-15-607 was found. Whether a tie is decided by the straw draw at the general election or only after a second election is not stated in either section [inferred: the straw draw applies to whichever count leaves candidates 'standing highest on the list, and not elected' with equal votes]. 23-15-981 has no tie clause of its own.

ties.applies_to: justice court judges, in the general election
ties.steps: section 23-15-193(3) sends the runoff elections of justice court judges to section 23-15-981: a candidate with a majority of the votes cast is elected; if none has one, the two with the most votes go on the ballot for a second election four weeks later 'in accordance with appropriate procedures followed in other elections involving runoff candidates'

sources.quote: The provisions of Section 23-15-981 shall control the runoff elections of justice court judges.

If no candidate for such office receives a majority of the votes cast for such office in the general election, the names of the two (2) candidates receiving the highest number of votes for such office shall be placed on the ballot for a second election to be held [...] four (4) weeks later in accordance with appropriate procedures followed in other elections involving runoff candidates.

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-193(3) (HB 291, 2025) and 23-15-981 (SB 2144, 2024). 23-15-981 has no tie clause for the second election; whether the coin or lot clause of 23-15-193(2) reaches a justice court judge's tie after that election is not stated, because subsection (3) says 23-15-981 'shall control' the runoff [inferred: unresolved].

ties.applies_to: municipal offices in the municipal general election
ties.steps: the municipal election commissioners canvass the returns the day after the election; if candidates receiving the highest number of votes have an equal number of votes, the election is decided by a toss of a coin or by lot fairly and publicly drawn under the direction of the election commissioners

sources.quote: If it shall appear that any two (2) or more of the candidates receiving the highest number of votes shall have received an equal number of votes, the election shall be decided by a toss of a coin or by lot [...] fairly and publicly drawn [...] under the direction of the election commissioners

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-611(1) as the 2017 revision (HB 467) prints it; no later act amending it was found. The majority-and-runoff rule of 23-15-193 is for the state general election and does not name municipal offices. Municipal charters were not read.

ties.applies_to: a special election to fill a vacancy in a municipal office (city, town or village) of more than six months' unexpired term
ties.steps: a candidate needs a majority; if none has one, the top two go on the ballot for an election three weeks later (a tie for the next highest vote sends all of those tied and the highest candidate to it); if that election is itself tied, a toss of a coin or a lot fairly and publicly drawn decides, under the supervision of the election commission

sources.quote: the two (2) candidates receiving the highest number of votes shall have their names placed on the ballot for the election to be held [...] three (3) weeks thereafter
result in a tie vote, the prevailing candidate [...] shall be decided by a toss of a coin or by lot [...] fairly and publicly drawn under the supervision [...] of the election commission

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-857(2) as HB 467 (2017) prints it. The long title of SB 2144 (2024), which moved runoffs to four weeks, lists 23-15-857 among the sections it amends, but the body of the act as sent to the Governor (read whole) has no section amending 23-15-857, so the three weeks stand unless another act changed it [inferred from the absence in the body].

ties.applies_to: a special election to fill a vacancy in a county, county district or district attorney office, or the office of circuit judge or chancellor
ties.steps: a candidate needs a majority; if none has one, a runoff is held four weeks after the election between the two with the most votes; a tie in the first election for the next highest vote sends those two and the highest candidate to the runoff, and whoever leads in the runoff is entitled to the office

sources.quote: where no candidate receives a majority of the votes cast in the election, a runoff election shall be held [...] four (4) weeks after the election.

When there is a tie in the first election of those receiving the next highest vote, these two (2) and the one receiving the highest vote, none having received a majority, shall go into the runoff election and whoever leads in the runoff election shall be entitled to the office.

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-833 as SB 2144 (2024) amends it (four weeks from 1 January 2025). A tie in the runoff itself is not addressed in the section; it says special elections are held 'in the same manner as general elections' apart from the runoff, which may bring in the coin or lot clause of 23-15-193(2) [inferred; not stated].

ties.applies_to: a party primary for a state, congressional, district or county office, and for U.S. Senator (nominated at the congressional primary)
ties.steps: a candidate with a majority of the votes cast is the nominee; if none has one, the two with the most votes go on the ballot for a second primary four weeks later, and whoever receives the most votes there is the nominee; if the tie is for the next highest vote, all of those tied and the highest candidate go into the second primary

sources.quote: If no candidate receives a majority vote at the election, then the two (2) candidates who receive the highest number of votes shall have their names placed on the ballot for the second primary election to be held [...] four (4) weeks later.

However, if no candidate receives a majority vote at the first primary, and there is a tie in the election of those receiving the next highest vote, then those candidates receiving the next highest vote and the candidate receiving the highest vote shall have their names placed on the ballot for the second primary election to be held [...] four (4) weeks later, and whoever receives the most votes cast in the second primary election shall be the party nominee.
and a second primary, if necessary, shall be held four (4) weeks thereafter.

Candidates for United States Senator shall be nominated at the congressional primary next preceding the general election at which a senator is to be elected and in the same manner that [...] Representatives in the Congress of the United States are nominated.

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-191 as SB 2144 (2024) amends it (four weeks from 1 January 2025; three weeks before) and 23-15-1031 as HB 293 (2025) amends it (the congressional primary now on the second Tuesday in March in years without a presidential election).

ties.steps: a majority nominates; if none has one, the top two go on the ballot for a second primary (on the fourth Tuesday in April preceding the general municipal election); if the tie is for the next highest vote, all of those tied and the highest candidate go into the second primary, and whoever receives the most votes there is the nominee

sources.quote: However, if no candidate shall receive a majority vote at the first primary, and there is a tie in the election of those receiving the next highest vote, those candidates receiving the next highest vote and the candidate receiving the highest vote shall have their names placed on the ballot for the second primary election, and whoever receives the most votes cast in the second primary election shall be the party nominee.
such second primary shall be held on the [...] fourth Tuesday in [...] April preceding such general municipal election

ties.note: Miss. Code 23-15-171(1) as the 2017 revision (HB 467) prints it. The long title of SB 2144 (2024) lists 23-15-171, but the body of that act has no section amending it, so the date and the absence of a four-week figure here are as in 2017 [inferred from the absence in the body]. Municipal charters that fix their own dates (171(2)) were not read.

ties.applies_to: a tie in the second primary
ties.steps: no provision for a tie at the end of the second primary was found
ties.note: Read: 23-15-191 and 23-15-1031 (SB 2144 and HB 293), 23-15-171 (HB 467); the only tie clauses in them are for the first primary. The Secretary of State's printing of Chapter 15 (2017) was searched for 'tie' and 'equal number of votes' with the same result; its case notes mention a tied second primary for a municipal office (Omar v. West, 1939) and a primary contest in which the court found equal votes, so that 'there was a tie and neither candidate is the nominee' (Hopkins v. Wilson, 1951); they are court decisions, not the statute, and were not relied on. The rules of the political parties were not read.

ties.applies_to: the electors of President and Vice President, chosen by the voters of the state at large
ties.steps: no tie provision for electors was found
ties.note: Read in the Secretary of State's 2017 printing of Chapter 15: 23-15-781 (electors chosen by the qualified electors of the state at large) and 23-15-783 (the laws regulating general elections apply to the election of electors) [stated], and the whole of Chapter 15 for 'tie', 'equal number of votes' and 'lot'; and, at the Legislature, 23-15-605 as HB 291 (2025) prints it, whose tie clause names a 'district office' of two or more counties, which an at-large office is not. Whether Title 23 outside Chapter 15 says more was not read.

ties.applies_to: a tie vote on a ballot measure
ties.steps: no provision for a tie on a ballot measure was found
ties.note: Read: a search of the whole of Chapter 15 as the Secretary of State printed it in 2017 (for 'tie', 'equal number of votes', 'lot' and 'coin'), and the acts of the Legislature read for this reading (none concerns a measure). The initiative and referendum provisions and section 273 of the Constitution were not read.

threshold.in_words: no recount of the votes, automatic or on request, with or without a margin, was found in the Election Code or in the acts of the Legislature read; the routes to a new look at the ballots are a candidate's examination of the ballot boxes and an election contest (the rules that follow)

sources.quote: the Commission does not have the authority to reassemble and alter or amend the certification of the results of the election. Any error which may be made in the canvass of the returns only may be corrected by a court of competent jurisdiction.

No audit shall occur until after a ballot box examination has occurred and the period to contest an election has expired, or if a runoff election occurs, the audit shall occur after the runoff election.

recounts.note: An absence, not a finding that no rule exists. Searched for 'recount', 're-count', 'recanvass' and 'reexamin' in the whole of Chapter 15 as the Secretary of State printed it in 2017. The statute text has the word only in the voting-equipment sections, where a direct recording machine must keep a paper record 'available for any recount' and be able to print the ballots 'in the event of a recount', which sets no recount; the other hits are in case notes and Attorney General opinions (a county party committee's recount of votes, a recount inside a contest, a court's mandate for 'a hand recount of ballots'), which are not the statute. Also searched for 'recount' in the text of the acts of the Legislature read, as they were sent to the Governor: HB 467 (2017; its two hits are the same voting-equipment words); HB 804, HB 937 (2018); HB 654, SB 2030 (2019); HB 1521 (2020); HB 1510, SB 2879 (2022); HB 1276, HB 1306, HB 1310, SB 2358 (2023); HB 1035, HB 1135, SB 2144, SB 2425 (2024); HB 291, HB 293, HB 724, HB 811, SB 2659 (2025); HB 859, HB 908, SB 2588 (2026): none of the others contains it. The quotation from the Secretary of State's 2026 handbook tells commissions they cannot reopen their certification and that a court corrects canvass errors. The 2023 audit (23-15-615, new) lets the Secretary of State audit election procedures in all 82 counties (in no more than a quarter of the precincts, or five, in each) after the box-examination and contest periods; it audits procedures, not the count, cannot be asked for, and is not a recount.

recounts.election: general or special election, county offices and state district offices (district attorney and the like)

threshold.conditions: a petition filed within twenty days after the election in the office of the circuit clerk of the county; the Chief Justice (or another Justice) has a circuit judge or chancellor of another district designated to hear it; a jury is made up and decides, and the verdict finds the person having the greatest number of legal votes or, for county and county district officers, a majority of legal votes
threshold.in_words: any person who wants to contest the election of another may file a petition within twenty days; no margin is required

who_may_request: a person desiring to contest the election of another person returned as elected to an office within the county
recounts.cost_bearer: costs are awarded as in other cases (by the court)

sources.quote: a person desiring to contest the election of another person returned as elected to any office within any county, may, within twenty (20) days after the election, file a petition in the office of the clerk of the circuit court of the county, setting forth the grounds upon which the election is contested.

the verdict of the jury shall find the person having the greatest number of legal votes at the election or the person having a majority of legal votes at the election, for county and county district officers
Each party shall be allowed ten (10) peremptory challenges, and new trials shall be granted and costs awarded as in other cases.

In case the election of district attorney or other state district election be contested, the petition may be filed in any county of the district or in any county of an adjoining district within twenty (20) days after the election

recounts.note: Miss. Code 23-15-951 as HB 291 (2025) amends it (in force 1 July 2025; the words 'or the person having a majority of legal votes at the election, for county and county district officers' came with the new majority rule). Not called a recount: the trial finds the legal votes. Recorded as the court route because it is the one way the ballots are counted again. Contests of the offices elected statewide (Governor and the other statewide officers) were not found in the sections read; 23-15-951 speaks of offices 'within any county' and state district offices.

recounts.election: general or special election to the Legislature

threshold.conditions: an election contest filed with the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate within thirty days after a regular general election (ten days after a special election to fill a vacancy)
threshold.in_words: the House or the Senate, not a court, has exclusive jurisdiction over a contest of its own member's seat; no margin is required

sources.quote: A person desiring to contest the election of another person returned as elected to any seat in the Mississippi Legislature shall comply with the provisions of Section 23-15-955.

the House of Representatives shall have exclusive jurisdiction over an election contest regarding the seat of any member of the House of Representatives, and the Senate shall have exclusive jurisdiction over an election contest regarding the seat of any member of the Senate.

An election contest regarding the seat of a member of the House of Representatives or the Senate shall be filed with the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate, as the case may be, within thirty (30) days after a regular general election

recounts.note: Miss. Code 23-15-955 (the Secretary of State's 2017 printing; no act printing it was found, so it is [stated]), citing Constitution section 38, and the pointer to it in 23-15-951 as HB 291 (2025) amends it [measured]. Type 'court' is the closest of the allowed types; the body that decides is the legislative chamber. 23-15-911(2) lets the ballot-box examination below be used in such a contest, with the result reported to the chamber.

threshold.conditions: a petition to the party executive committee within twenty days after the primary (23-15-921: county and county-district nominations, and legislative districts of one county or less); for state, congressional and judicial districts and legislative districts of more than one county, a complaint by petition with the chairman of the State Executive Committee (23-15-923, which states no number of days itself); the committee declares the true result by majority vote of the members present; if the committee fails to act or unreasonably delays, the contestant may file a petition for judicial review in the circuit court within ten days after the contest was filed, on the certificate of two practicing attorneys and a $300 cost bond (23-15-927)
threshold.in_words: any person who wants to contest a nomination may petition the party executive committee (within twenty days after the primary, for county nominations); no margin is required; the contest can then go to the circuit court

who_may_request: a person desiring to contest the election of another returned as the nominee
recounts.cost_bearer: the petitioner for judicial review gives a $300 cost bond to pay the costs if the petition is dismissed (23-15-927); the committee's own costs are not stated in the sections read

sources.quote: a person desiring to contest the election of another person returned as the nominee of the party to any county or county district office, or as the nominee of a legislative district composed of one (1) county or less, may, within twenty (20) days after the primary election, file a petition with the secretary, or any member of the county executive committee in the county in which the election was held
The State Executive Committee by majority vote of members present shall declare the true results of such primary.
A petition for judicial review must be filed within ten (10) days after any contest or complaint has been filed with an executive committee.
The petitioner shall give a cost bond in the sum of Three Hundred Dollars ($300.00), with two (2) or more sufficient sureties conditioned to pay all costs in case his petition be dismissed

recounts.note: Miss. Code 23-15-921, 23-15-923 and 23-15-927 in the Secretary of State's 2017 printing (no act printing them was found). Applies to the nomination, not to a recount by name. The sections after 23-15-927 (23-15-929 to 23-15-941: the circuit judge's designation, appeal, expenses) are not recorded here.

threshold.conditions: within twelve days after the canvass of the box by the election commission or executive committee, on three days' notice served on the opposing candidates; the examination is made in the presence of the circuit clerk or a deputy, and the box is resealed
threshold.in_words: any candidate, or a representative authorized in writing, may examine the ballot box and its contents within twelve days after the canvass; no margin is required; it is an examination, not a count by officials

who_may_request: any candidate, or a representative authorized in writing by the candidate

sources.quote: At any time within twelve (12) days after the canvass and examination of the box and its contents by the election commission or executive committee, as the case may be
any candidate or his or her representative authorized in writing by him or her shall have the right of full examination of [...] the box and its contents upon three (3) days' notice
The provisions of this section allowing the examination of ballot boxes shall apply in the case of an election contest regarding the seat of a member of the state Legislature.

recounts.note: Miss. Code 23-15-911(1)(a) and (2) as the 2017 revision (HB 467) prints it; no later act amending it was found. It is what a candidate does before a contest (the 2023 audit section, 23-15-615, still assumes 'a ballot box examination has occurred' before it runs). It gives a look at the ballots, not an official recount; the section sets no margin and no cost.

notes: What a reader of the law would not expect: (1) since 1 January 2025 a runoff, and since 1 July 2025 a majority, is needed in the state general election for every office of Miss. Code 23-15-193(1), not only for state officers: House Bill 291 (2025) changed 'the state officers that receive a majority' to 'the candidate that receives a majority', and a tie after the runoff goes to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court for a coin toss or lot (23-15-193(2)); (2) the straw draw (longer of two straws from an opaque bag, drawn under the direction of the Governor and the Secretary of State) remains for a U.S. Representative, a legislative district of two or more counties, and a Supreme Court or Court of Appeals judge; (3) Mississippi has no recount in the Election Code as far as read: a candidate may examine the ballot boxes within twelve days of the canvass (23-15-911), and may bring a contest within twenty days (thirty for a legislative seat, to the chamber itself).

The Governor's tie rule is a rule of the Code, not of the Constitution. Section 140 of the Constitution, as the Legislature's resolution HC 47 (2020) proposed it, gives the office to the person with a majority and leaves any runoff to 'procedures prescribed by the Legislature in general law'; it repeals section 141, under which the House of Representatives chose between the top two. The runoff and the Chief Justice's coin or lot are 23-15-193(2). Whether the voters adopted HC 47 was not read (see unread).

How amendments after the 2017 printing were looked for: I read the lists of all measures of the 2017 to 2026 regular sessions and the extraordinary sessions of 2017, 2018, 2022, 2024 (two), 2025 and 2026 on the Legislature's bill-status host, and the lists of measures referred to the House Apportionment and Elections and Senate Elections committees of 2018 to 2026, and kept the ones that became law and whose short titles name elections, ballots, voting, candidates, primaries, runoffs, contests or similar; I fetched the text of 24 of them (HB 467 of 2017; HB 804 and HB 937 of 2018; HB 654 and SB 2030 of 2019; HB 1521 of 2020; HB 1510 and SB 2879 of 2022; HB 1276, HB 1306, HB 1310 and SB 2358 of 2023; HB 1035, HB 1135, SB 2144 and SB 2425 of 2024; HB 291, HB 293, HB 724, HB 811 and SB 2659 of 2025; HB 859, HB 908 and SB 2588 of 2026) and read the long title and the sections of each that touch Chapter 15. The limit: a measure that amended a section read here but whose short title says nothing of elections would have been missed, and the Code's own present text (at LexisNexis) was not read; so 'no later act found' means no such act in those lists. The acts that print the sections used are HB 467 (2017), SB 2144 (2024), HB 293 and HB 291 (2025).

Before House Bill 291 (2025) the county tie rule of the Secretary of State's 2017 printing and 2026 handbook gave a tie for a county office, the board of supervisors, a justice court judge or a constable to the county election commissioners for a coin toss or lot (23-15-601). HB 291 struck those offices from that clause and moved them to the majority-and-runoff rule; the 2026 handbook's statement of the old rule predates it in substance.

Where 23-15-601 and 23-15-605 (tie clauses for legislative seats) and 23-15-193(2) (runoff, then the Chief Justice) overlap, HB 291 amended or brought forward all of them and does not say which controls. Both are recorded.
